questions.question: Newton's First Law of Motion is also known as the:
questions.explanation: Newton's first law describes how bodies resist changes in motion, so it is called the Law of Inertia. The Law of Acceleration is the second law, Action and Reaction is the third, and Universal Gravitation is a separate law.

questions.question: A body is said to be in equilibrium when the net external force acting on it is:
questions.explanation: A body is in translational equilibrium when the net external force is zero, so it is at rest or moves with constant velocity.

questions.question: The tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of motion is called:
questions.explanation: Inertia is the property of matter by which a body resists any change in its state of rest or uniform motion.

questions.question: Which of the following is a quantitative measure of inertia?
questions.explanation: Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia: the greater the mass, the greater the resistance to change in motion.

questions.question: A passenger lurches forward when a moving bus suddenly stops. This is best explained by:
options: The law of conservation of energy
questions.explanation: When the bus stops, the passenger's body tends to keep moving forward because of inertia — this is Newton's First Law.

questions.question: A reference frame in which Newton's First Law holds true is called a(n):
questions.explanation: An inertial reference frame is a non-accelerating frame in which Newton's first law (and the other laws in their simple form) holds.

questions.question: Newton's Second Law states that the rate of change of linear momentum is directly proportional to the:
options: net external force acting on it
questions.explanation: Newton's second law in general form: Fnet = dp ÷ dt, so the rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the net external force.

questions.question: The SI unit of force, the newton (N), is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: Since F = ma, one newton = 1 kg × 1 m s−2 = kg m s−2.

questions.question: If the mass of a body is constant, Newton's Second Law can be written as:
questions.explanation: For constant mass, F = dp ÷ dt reduces to F = ma.

questions.question: According to Newton's Second Law, the acceleration of an object is inversely proportional to its:
questions.explanation: From a = F ÷ m, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass for a given net force.

questions.question: In an action-reaction pair, the two forces:
options: have the same magnitude and direction
questions.explanation: Action-reaction pairs act on different bodies, which is why they do not cancel. They are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a contact force?
questions.explanation: Frictional force requires contact between surfaces. Gravitational, magnetic, and electrostatic forces act at a distance.

questions.question: The normal force exerted by a surface on an object acts:
questions.explanation: The normal force acts perpendicular to the surface of contact.

questions.question: The term 'normal' in 'normal force' originates from geometry and means:
questions.explanation: In geometry, 'normal' means perpendicular — hence the normal force is perpendicular to the surface.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about mass is correct?
questions.explanation: Mass is a scalar quantity, measured in kilograms, and is constant everywhere.

questions.question: Weight is best defined as:
options: the amount of matter in a body
the gravitational force on a body
questions.explanation: Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body: W = mg. It is a vector measured in newtons.

questions.question: An object has a mass of 5 kg on Earth. On the Moon, its mass will be:
questions.explanation: Mass is an intrinsic property and does not change with location, so on the Moon the mass is still 5 kg. Only weight changes.

questions.question: The weight of an object on Earth is 49 N. On the Moon (g = 1.6 m s<sup>−2</sup>), its weight will be approximately:
questions.explanation: Mass = W ÷ g = 49 ÷ 9.8 = 5 kg. On the Moon, W = mg = 5 × 1.6 = 8 N.

questions.question: For a box on a frictionless inclined plane, the component of weight along the plane is:
questions.explanation: Along a plane inclined at θ, the sliding component of weight is mg sin θ; the perpendicular component is mg cos θ.

questions.question: On a frictionless inclined plane, the normal force is equal in magnitude to:
questions.explanation: The normal force balances the perpendicular component of weight, so N = mg cos θ.

questions.question: In a frictionless Atwood machine with masses m<sub>1</sub> and m<sub>2</sub> (m<sub>2</sub> > m<sub>1</sub>), the acceleration of the system is:
options: (m2 − m1)gm1 + m2
(m1 + m2)gm2 − m1
questions.explanation: Solving the coupled equations T − m1g = m1a and m2g − T = m2a gives a = (m2 − m1)g ÷ (m1 + m2).

questions.question: Two blocks in contact on a frictionless horizontal surface are pushed by a horizontal force. The force that block A exerts on block B is:
questions.explanation: The applied force accelerates both blocks; the contact force only accelerates block B, so it is less than the applied force.

questions.question: For a block pulled along a horizontal frictionless floor by a cord at an angle θ to the horizontal, the vertical component of the tension:
options: has no effect on the normal force
equals the weight of the block
questions.explanation: The upward vertical component of the tension reduces the normal force: N = mg − T sin θ. So it reduces the normal force.

questions.question: Just before a block is lifted completely off the floor by an upward cord, the normal force becomes:
questions.explanation: When the block is just about to lift off, the normal force drops to zero and the tension alone balances the weight.

questions.question: If the net force acting on an object is constant and non-zero, the object undergoes:
questions.explanation: A constant net force produces a constant acceleration, so the object undergoes uniform acceleration (F = ma).

questions.question: Which law explains why a rocket is propelled forward by ejecting gas backward?
questions.explanation: The rocket pushes gas backward and the gas pushes the rocket forward — an equal and opposite pair. This is Newton's Third Law.

questions.question: A body moving with constant velocity in a straight line has:
options: zero net force acting on it
a constant net force acting on it
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero.

questions.question: The inertia of an object depends on its:
questions.explanation: Inertia is measured by mass: the greater the mass, the greater the inertia.

questions.question: Which of the following forces is NOT a fundamental force of nature?
questions.explanation: The normal force is a contact (reaction) force, not a fundamental force. The four fundamental forces are gravitational, electromagnetic, strong, and weak nuclear.

questions.question: A scalar quantity has:
questions.explanation: A scalar has magnitude only, with no direction.

questions.question: A vector quantity has:
questions.explanation: A vector has both magnitude and direction.

questions.question: The resultant of two forces acting on a body is found by:
options: subtracting the smaller from the larger
questions.explanation: Forces are vectors, so their resultant is found by vector addition (e.g. parallelogram or component method).

questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface is approximately:
questions.explanation: Near Earth's surface, g ≈ 9.8 m s−2. (1.6 is the Moon's g, 6.7 × 10−11 is G, and 3.0 × 108 is the speed of light.)

questions.question: If the same force is applied to two objects of different masses, the object with the smaller mass will have:
questions.explanation: Since a = F ÷ m, for the same F a smaller mass gives a larger acceleration.

questions.question: When a body moves with uniform circular motion, its acceleration is directed:
options: toward the center of the circle
questions.explanation: Uniform circular motion has centripetal acceleration toward the center of the circle.

questions.question: The force responsible for keeping a body in circular motion is called:
questions.explanation: The centripetal force is the net inward force that keeps a body in circular motion.

questions.question: A block is at rest on a rough horizontal surface. The force that opposes its impending motion is:
questions.explanation: Before motion begins, the opposing force is static friction, which adjusts up to a maximum value.

questions.question: Once a block starts sliding on a rough surface, the friction acting on it is:
questions.explanation: While sliding, the friction is kinetic friction, roughly constant and generally less than the maximum static friction.

questions.question: The coefficient of kinetic friction is generally:
options: greater than the coefficient of static friction
equal to the coefficient of static friction
less than the coefficient of static friction
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction is usually less than static friction, so μk < μs for the same pair of surfaces.

questions.question: The principle of inertia implies that a net external force is required to:
questions.explanation: By inertia, a body maintains its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a net force; hence a net force is required to change velocity.
